questions.q: What five elements does this lesson say a credible fine-tuning write-up should include?
options: Only the final task metric, with no other context
A problem statement, model/data choices and why, the training configuration and what happened during the run, evaluation results against a baseline, and known limitations
A list of every hyperparameter tried during experimentation, with no narrative
Only a screenshot of the training loss curve
questions.explain: The lesson lists these five elements in order: problem statement, model/data choices and reasoning, training configuration and run behavior, baseline-relative evaluation results, and known limitations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against leading with the task-metric win while burying or omitting the general-capability delta?
options: Because the general-capability delta is always zero and therefore not worth mentioning

Because a write-up with both numbers, even when the regression is real, is more credible and useful than one with only the flattering number -- this is the same discipline built in the catastrophic forgetting and evaluation lessons
Because task metrics are never reliable and should be excluded entirely
Because general-capability deltas cannot be computed for LoRA-based fine-tunes
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties this back to the catastrophic forgetting and evaluation lessons: reporting both the win and the regression honestly is more credible than showcasing only the favorable number.

questions.q: How does this lesson suggest the write-up connect back to Chapter 8's serving material, even without a real production deployment?
options: By ignoring serving considerations entirely since no real deployment occurred
By including a rough serving cost estimate, a quantization recommendation suited to the measured accuracy delta, and the shape of a handoff package, as proof the Chapter 8 skills transferred
By requiring an actual vLLM deployment before the capstone can be considered complete
By replacing the evaluation results with serving latency numbers instead
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends writing a serving-aware section covering cost estimation, a quantization recommendation, and a handoff package shape, as the way to demonstrate the Chapter 8 material actually transferred, even without deploying the capstone model.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as usually the single highest-leverage next step for improving a narrow fine-tune, ahead of hyperparameter tuning?
options: Switching to a completely different base model architecture
More and better data
Increasing the LoRA rank to the maximum supported value
Disabling prompt masking to speed up training
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that more and better data is almost always the highest-leverage change for most narrow fine-tunes, ahead of hyperparameter tuning.

questions.q: What does this final lesson say carries forward even though the course's structured material ends here?
options: Nothing; the skills taught are only relevant within this specific capstone project
The discipline of justifying decisions with evidence, evaluating honestly, and knowing enough about the next stage of the pipeline to hand off well
Only the specific model and dataset used in this exact capstone
The requirement to always use exactly the same base model in future projects
questions.explain: The lesson closes by stating that the discipline built across the course -- evidence-based decisions, honest evaluation, and handoff awareness -- is what carries forward into real training or ML systems work, beyond the specific course material.
